items.title: The Sobolev conjugate exponent and the scaling identity
items.statement:
Let $n\ge2$ and $1\le p<n$. The **Sobolev conjugate** of $p$ is
$$p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}.$$
The denominator $n-p$ is positive, so $p^{*}$ is a finite real number greater
than $1$. Conjugate exponents in the sense of
[[def-conjugate-exponents]] and real powers in the sense of
[[def-real-power]] are used below.

The following elementary identities are part of the definition and record how
$p^{*}$ is used.
$$\frac{1}{p^{*}}=\frac{n-p}{np}=\frac1p-\frac1n,\qquad p^{*}-p=\frac{np-p(n-p)}{n-p}=\frac{p^{2}}{n-p}>0,$$
so $p^{*}>p$ and $1/p^{*}+1/n=1/p$; in particular $p^{*}=n/(n-1)$ when $p=1$.
Equivalently $p^{*}=n\big/\big(\frac np-1\big)$.

For $k\ge1$ with $kp<n$ the **$k$-fold Sobolev conjugate** $p^{*}_{k}$ is
defined recursively by
$$\frac{1}{p^{*}_{1}}=\frac1p-\frac1n,\qquad \frac{1}{p^{*}_{j+1}}=\frac{1}{p^{*}_{j}}-\frac1n\quad(1\le j<k).$$
Induction on $j$ gives $\frac1{p^{*}_{j}}=\frac1p-\frac jn$ and hence
$$p^{*}_{k}=\frac{np}{n-kp};$$
the recursion is well posed because $jp<n$ for $j\le k$ keeps every
$p^{*}_{j}$ finite and greater than $1$.

Finally, the map $p\mapsto p^{*}=n/(\frac np-1)$ is continuous on $(1,n)$,
since $n/p-1>0$ there and the reciprocal and affine maps are continuous; it is
strictly increasing on $(1,n)$, because $p\mapsto n/p$ is strictly decreasing
and $t\mapsto n/(t-1)$ is strictly decreasing on $(1,\infty)$; and
$p^{*}\to\infty$ as $p\to n^{-}$, because $n/p-1\to0^{+}$. No finite Sobolev
conjugate is attached to $p\ge n$: for $p=n$ the formula has denominator $0$,
and for $p>n$ the expression $np/(n-p)$ is negative.
items.strategy: Direct algebra with reciprocals and real powers using $n-p>0$; both displayed identities are rearrangements of $p^{*}=np/(n-p)$. The recursion is induction on $j$ and gives $\frac1{p^{*}_k}=\frac1p-\frac k n$; monotonicity and the limit follow by differentiating or by rewriting $p^{*}=n\big/(\frac n p-1)$.

items.title: Pointwise potential bound for compactly supported smooth functions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and $u\in C_c^{\infty}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $|u(x)|\le\frac1{\sigma(S^{n-1})}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|Du(y)|\,|x-y|^{1-n}\,dy$, where $\sigma$ is the polar surface measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]] and $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the gradient. In particular $|u(x)|\le C(n)\int_{\mathbb R^n}|Du(y)|\,|x-y|^{1-n}dy$.
items.strategy: Fix $x$ and $\omega\in S^{n-1}$. Since $u$ is smooth and compactly supported, $t\mapsto u(x+t\omega)$ is absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with value $0$ at $+\infty$, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $|u(x)|\le\int_0^{\infty}|Du(x+t\omega)|\,dt$. Integrate in $\omega$ against $\sigma$: the left side contributes $|u(x)|\sigma(S^{n-1})$, and the translated polar-coordinates formula for Lebesgue measure (translation invariance plus the rotation-invariant polar decomposition) rewrites the right side as $\int_{\mathbb R^n}|Du(y)|\,|x-y|^{1-n}dy$. Positivity and finiteness of $\sigma(S^{n-1})$ follow from the defining relation $\sigma(S^{n-1})=n\lambda(B(0,1))$.

items.title: The p=1 Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$. There is a constant $C(n)$ such that $\|u\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(n)\,\|Du\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}$ for every $u\in C_c^{\infty}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$.
items.strategy: For each $j$ the fundamental theorem of calculus and compact support give $|u(x)|\le\int_{\mathbb R}|\partial_ju(x_1,\dots,t,\dots,x_n)|\,dt$ for every $x$. Multiply the $n$ pointwise inequalities and take the $(n-1)$-th root: $|u(x)|^{n/(n-1)}\le\prod_{j=1}^n\big(\int_{\mathbb R}|\partial_ju|\,dt_j\big)^{1/(n-1)}$. Integrate successively over $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$; at step $j$ apply the generalized Hölder inequality to the product of the $n-1$ remaining factors, each of which is an $L^1$ function of the free variables; Tonelli's theorem justifies the iterated integrals. The result is $\|u\|_{n/(n-1)}^{n/(n-1)}\le\prod_j\int_{\mathbb R^n}|Du|=\|Du\|_1^{n/(n-1)}$.

items.title: The Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality for $1<p<n$
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is a constant $C(n,p)$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C(n,p)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$; here $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the weak gradient.
items.strategy: For smooth compactly supported real u, choose a smooth compact cutoff equal to one near supp u and apply the p=1 GNS inequality to chi(u^2+delta^2)^(gamma/2). The cutoff-gradient contribution is delta^gamma Dchi and vanishes; dominated convergence gives the |u|^gamma limit and the gradient integral. Holder with (gamma-1)p/(p-1)=p* yields the real estimate; split into real and imaginary parts for complex u. Extend to W^{1,p} by compactly supported smooth density, applying the smooth estimate to differences and using L^{p*} completeness and an almost-everywhere subsequence.

items.title: The Sobolev inequality for zero-boundary Sobolev closures on open sets
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is $C(n,p)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C(n,p)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.
items.strategy: Let $\tilde u$ be the zero extension of $u$; it lies in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ with $D\tilde u=Du$ on $\Omega$ and $D\tilde u=0$ off $\Omega$, so both norms are unchanged. Since $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is by definition the closure of $C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)$ and the zero extensions of $C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)$ functions are compactly supported smooth functions, approximate $\tilde u$ in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ by compactly supported smooth functions and apply the whole-space inequality to the approximations and their differences, exactly as in the density step of [[thm-gagliardo-nirenberg-sobolev-inequality]].

items.title: Poincare inequality on a ball
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, $B=B(x_0,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $r>0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and $u\in W^{1,p}(B;\mathbb K)$ with ball average $u_B=|B|^{-1}\int_Bu$. Then $\|u-u_B\|_{L^p(B)}\le C(n,p)\,r\,\|Du\|_{L^p(B)}$.
items.strategy: Translation and dilation reduce to $B=B(0,r)$; by local smooth approximation it suffices to treat $u\in C^{\infty}(B)\cap W^{1,p}(B)$ and pass to the limit in $W^{1,p}$. (i) For $x,y\in B$ the segment $[x,y]$ lies in the ball and the fundamental theorem gives $|u(x)-u(y)|^p\le|x-y|^p\int_0^1|Du(x+t(y-x))|^pdt$. (ii) Integrate in $y$ in polar coordinates $y=x+s\omega$ centred at $x$: the radial range satisfies $s\le2r$, and the substitution $\rho=ts$ turns the inner integral into $\int_0^s|Du(x+\rho\omega)|^pd\rho$, so $\int_0^{s_{\max}}s^{p+n-2}\int_0^s|Du(x+\rho\omega)|^pd\rho\,ds\le Cr^{p+n-1}\int_B|Du(z)|^p|x-z|^{1-n}dz$ with all integration confined to $B$. (iii) Integrate over $x\in B$ and use $\int_B|x-z|^{1-n}dx\le C(n)r$ to get $\int_B\int_B|u(x)-u(y)|^p\le Cr^{p+n}\|Du\|_{L^p(B)}^p$. (iv) Jensen (Hölder with the probability measure $|B|^{-1}dx$) gives $\int_B|u-u_B|^p\le|B|^{-1}\int_B\int_B|u(x)-u(y)|^p$, and $|B|=c_nr^n$ yields the claim.

items.title: The Poincare inequality for zero-boundary Sobolev closures on domains bounded in one direction
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.
items.strategy: Rotate so that $e=e_n$ and $\Omega\subset\{a<x_n<b\}$. For $u\in C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)$, the fundamental theorem in the $x_n$ direction and compact support give $|u(x)|\le\int_a^b|\partial_nu(x',t)|dt$; Hölder gives $|u(x)|^p\le(b-a)^{p-1}\int_a^b|\partial_nu(x',t)|^pdt$. Integrate over $\Omega$, extend the $x_n$-integral over $(a,b)$ for each $x'$ and apply Tonelli: $\|u\|_p^p\le(b-a)^p\|Du\|_p^p$. The full class follows because $C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)$ is dense in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ by definition and both sides are continuous in the $W^{1,p}$-norm. The factor $2\operatorname{diam}$-type constants of the general statements are not needed here; boundedness in one direction suffices.

items.title: Mean-zero Poincare estimate on bounded connected extension domains below the dimension
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice (and hence Countable Choice and Dependent Choice). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected $W^{1,p}$-extension domain. Then there exists $C_P=C_P(n,p,\Omega,\mathbb K)$ such that $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_P\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u$.
items.strategy: Suppose the estimate fails. Countable Choice selects mean-zero $v_j$ with $\|v_j\|_p=1$ and $\|Dv_j\|_p<1/j$. Fix one bounded extension operator $E$ and a smooth compactly supported cutoff $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Put $F_j=\chi Ev_j$. By the extension bound and weak Leibniz rule there is $M$ with $\|F_j\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}\le M$, all $F_j$ have support in a common compact ball, and $F_j|_\Omega=v_j$. For smooth compactly supported $F$, the line FTC and Minkowski give $\|F(\cdot-h)-F\|_p\le |h|\|DF\|_p$; global smooth density passes this to every $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ class. Thus for the unit-mass radial mollifier supported in $B_\varepsilon$, Minkowski gives $\|F_j*\rho_\varepsilon-F_j\|_p\le\varepsilon M$. For each fixed $0<\varepsilon\le1$, differentiation under the convolution integral and Holder give uniform bounds $\|F_j*\rho_\varepsilon\|_\infty\le M\|\rho_\varepsilon\|_{p'}$ and $\|D(F_j*\rho_\varepsilon)\|_\infty\le M\|D\rho_\varepsilon\|_{p'}$. All convolutions have support in one fixed compact ball $K$. Arzela--Ascoli and metric sequential compactness give a uniformly convergent subsequence for this fixed epsilon; apply the real-valued theorem first to real and then to imaginary parts when needed. Using Dependent Choice, extract nested subsequences for $\varepsilon_m=2^{-m}$, then take a diagonal subsequence $F_{j_k}$. For fixed $m$, the smoothed diagonal tail is Cauchy in $L^p(K)$, and $\|F_{j_k}-F_{j_l}\|_p\le2M\varepsilon_m+\|F_{j_k}*\rho_{\varepsilon_m}-F_{j_l}*\rho_{\varepsilon_m}\|_p$. First choose $m$ large, then $k,l$ large: the diagonal is Cauchy in $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$, hence converges by Riesz--Fischer. Restriction gives $v_{j_k}\to v$ in $L^p(\Omega)$. Holder and norm continuity give $\int_\Omega v=0$ and $\|v\|_p=1$. For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, pass $\int v_{j_k}\partial_i\varphi=-\int\partial_iv_{j_k}\varphi$ to the limit using Holder and $Dv_{j_k}\to0$; this proves the weak derivatives of $v$ are zero, without asserting gradient norm convergence from Rellich alone. Connectedness and the published zero-gradient theorem imply $v$ is constant a.e., and its zero mean gives $v=0$, a contradiction. This is an internal compactness argument proved from published smoothing and Arzela--Ascoli interfaces; it uses no later PDE-15 supplier. No compactness-free proof is claimed. AC is inherited by the smooth-density interface; CC selects the contradicting sequence and DC selects nested subsequences.

items.title: John domains and the John constant
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, bounded and nonempty. Its boundary $\partial\Omega$ is then a nonempty
compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$ contained in a sufficiently large closed ball
([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]],
[[cor-euclidean-closed-balls-and-spheres-are-compact]]), and the distance
$\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ is defined for every $x$ and is a
$1$-Lipschitz function of $x$ ([[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]]).

Rectifiable curves, their arclength functions are used with the conventions of [[def-arc-length-function]].

**John domain and John constant.** A pair $(\Omega,x_0)$ with $x_0\in\Omega$
satisfies the **John condition** with constant $c\ge1$ if for every $x\in\Omega$
there is a rectifiable curve $\gamma:[0,l]\to\Omega$ parametrised by arclength,
with $\gamma(0)=x$, $\gamma(l)=x_0$ and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\gamma(t),\partial\Omega)\ge c^{-1}|x-\gamma(t)|\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,l].$$
Write $c_J(\Omega,x_0)$ for the infimum of the admissible constants $c\ge1$;
with the convention $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, this value belongs to $[1,+\infty]$. The domain $\Omega$ is a
**John domain** if $c_J(\Omega,x_0)<\infty$ for some $x_0\in\Omega$, and
$c_J(\Omega,x_0)$ is the **John constant of the pair** $(\Omega,x_0)$. The
estimates below use an admissible constant, never the finiteness of the
infimum alone, and whether the infimum is attained is immaterial.

**Arclength form.** If $\gamma$ is arclength parametrised from $x$, then
$t\ge|\gamma(t)-x|$ for $0\le t\le l$, because the straight segment from $x$ to
$\gamma(t)$ is no longer than the curve. Hence a curve satisfying the
arclength normalisation $\operatorname{dist}(\gamma(t),\partial\Omega)\ge
c^{-1}t$ for all $t$ also satisfies the displayed relative-distance condition
with the same constant $c$. Only this implication is used here; the chain construction below uses the displayed relative-distance condition.

**Connectedness.** A John domain is path-connected and hence connected: given
$x,y\in\Omega$, choose curves $\gamma_x$ from $x$ to $x_0$ and $\gamma_y$ from
$y$ to $x_0$ as in the definition (under Countable Choice the two curves may be
chosen simultaneously) and traverse $\gamma_x$ followed by the reverse of
$\gamma_y$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed beyond what the
definition uses.
items.strategy: No proof is required for the definition. The stated equivalence is immediate from $t\ge|x-\gamma(t)|$ in one direction and from the standard reparametrisation of a curve satisfying the relative-distance condition in the other.

items.title: Bounded-overlap ball chains in a bounded John domain
items.strategy: For x outside B(x0,2r0), choose a John curve and construct the chain by taking each next centre at the first boundary point encountered while moving along the curve toward x. The first pair has r0/(4cJ) <= r1 <= (1+1/(4cJ))r0; an intersection ball of radius r1/2 centred halfway from x1 toward x0 gives a ratio bound depending only on n,cJ. From the second transition onward, consecutive radii differ by factors between 3/4 and 5/4, so midpoint balls of radius ri/4 give uniform overlap bounds. The John condition gives the distance and convergence estimates, and a packing argument gives bounded multiplicity. For x in B(x0,2r0), use the explicit geometric chain with halving radii and multiplicity at most two. One John curve is selected for each x.

items.title: The truncated Riesz kernel is bounded on $L^p$ of a bounded set
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$, $\rho>0$, and let $\Omega\subseteq B(z_0,\rho)$ be measurable, $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then $\big\|\int_\Omega|x-y|^{1-n}|f(y)|\,dy\big\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n)\,\rho\,\|f\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$. In particular, for a bounded John domain the John condition gives $\operatorname{diam}\Omega\le c|\Omega|^{1/n}$, so the bound holds with coefficient $C(n,c_J)|\Omega|^{1/n}$.
items.strategy: Since $\Omega\subseteq B(z_0,\rho)$ one has $|x-y|\le2\rho$ for all $x,y\in\Omega$, so the kernel may be truncated: $Tf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}k(x-y)f(y)dy$ with $k(z)=|z|^{1-n}\mathbf 1_{B(0,2\rho)}(z)\in L^1$, $\|k\|_1=C(n)\rho$ (radial integration). Tonelli gives the strong $(1,1)$ bound $\|Tf\|_1\le\|k\|_1\|f\|_1$ and the pointwise estimate $|Tf(x)|\le\|k\|_1\|f\|_\infty$ gives the strong $(\infty,\infty)$ bound, hence a weak $(1,1)$ bound. Marcinkiewicz interpolation yields the strong $L^p$ bound with constant $C\|k\|_1$ for $1<p<\infty$, and $p=1$ is the Tonelli bound. For a bounded John domain, $\operatorname{diam}\Omega\le c(n,c_J)|\Omega|^{1/n}$ (the John condition at the distinguished point) lets one take $\rho=c(n,c_J)|\Omega|^{1/n}$ after covering $\Omega$ by such a ball.

items.title: The mean-zero Poincare inequality on bounded John domains
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded John domain with admissible constant $c_J$, and let $1\le p<\infty$. There is a constant $C(n,p,c_J)$ with
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,c_J)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u$. The factor $\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)$ is necessary: for the function $u(x)=x_1$ on a ball of radius $R$ with the centre as distinguished point, the ratio $\|u-u_B\|_{L^p(B)}/\|Du\|_{L^p(B)}$ grows linearly in $R$, while the John constant of that pair is $1$ for every $R$.
items.strategy: For almost every x, compare each John-chain ball B_i to the centered ball B(x,(M+2)r_i): the chain distance condition gives inclusion and the volume ratio is (M+2)^n, so Lebesgue differentiation yields u_{B_i}→u(x). Telescope the means from the reference ball, use ball Poincare and overlap to bound the pointwise difference by the truncated potential of |Du|, then apply the truncated-kernel Lp estimate and adjust the reference mean to u_Ω. A linear function on expanding centered balls shows the diameter factor is necessary.

items.title: The Poincare inequality with a positive-measure zero set
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded John domain with admissible constant $c_J$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $A\subseteq\Omega$ be measurable with $|A|\ge\gamma|\Omega|$ for some $\gamma\in(0,1]$. If $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere on $A$, then
$$\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,c_J,\gamma)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
items.strategy: Since $u$ vanishes a.e. on $A$, $|u_\Omega|\le\fint_\Omega|u|=\fint_{\Omega\setminus A}|u|$, and Hölder over the normalised measure on $\Omega\setminus A$ gives $|u_\Omega|\le(1-\gamma)^{1-1/p}\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for $p>1$ (and the direct bound for $p=1$). Write $\|u\|_p\le\|u-u_\Omega\|_p+|\Omega|^{1/p}|u_\Omega|$, bound the first term by the mean-zero Poincare inequality and absorb $(1-\gamma)^{1-1/p}\|u\|_p$ into the left side; the coefficient $1-(1-\gamma)^{1-1/p}$ is positive because $\gamma>0$.

items.title: Poincare-Wirtinger on bounded convex domains by the direct pairwise argument
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded, convex and nonempty, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Here $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx$ is the mean of $u$ over $\Omega$,
which is well defined because $\Omega$ is nonempty open and bounded. The proof
below gives the explicit choice
$$C(n)=\frac{2\,(2^n-1)}{n},$$
which depends only on the dimension; no dependence on $p$, on the shape of
$\Omega$, on $|\Omega|$ or on the regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is used.
items.strategy: Repeat the pairwise argument of [[thm-poincare-inequality-on-a-ball]] with the ball replaced by the convex set $\Omega$: for $x,y\in\Omega$ the segment $[x,y]$ lies in $\Omega$, so $|u(x)-u(y)|^p\le|x-y|^p\int_0^1|Du(x+t(y-x))|^pdt$; polar integration around $x$ has radial range at most $D=\operatorname{diam}\Omega$ and the weight satisfies $\int_\Omega|x-z|^{1-n}dz\le C(n)D$; integrating over $x,y$ and applying Jensen to the mean gives the claim. Smooth approximations extend the result to $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$.

items.title: Sobolev embedding on bounded extension domains for $p<n$
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$
items.strategy: Let $W=Eu$. The whole-space inequality [[thm-gagliardo-nirenberg-sobolev-inequality]] applied to $W$ gives $\|W\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|DW\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|E\|\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$; restricting to $\Omega$ and applying the transfer corollary gives the endpoint case $q=p^{*}$. For $p\le q\le p^{*}$ write $1/q=\theta/p+(1-\theta)/p^{*}$ with $\theta\in[0,1]$; Hölder on the finite-measure set $\Omega$ gives $\|u\|_q\le\|u\|_p^{\theta}\|u\|_{p^{*}}^{1-\theta}\le C\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$, since $\|u\|_p\le\|u\|_{W^{1,p}}$. Every bounded $C^k$ domain, $k\ge1$, supplies an admissible $E$ through the extension theorem cited in the transfer corollary.

items.title: Sobolev-Poincare on bounded connected extension domains
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice (and hence Countable Choice and Dependent Choice). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$, $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected $W^{1,p}$-extension domain. There is $C=C(n,p,\Omega,\mathbb K)$ such that every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u .$$
The domain constant is not uniform over arbitrary extension domains.
items.strategy: Holder on the finite positive measure domain makes the mean finite. Set $v=u-u_\Omega$; weak derivative linearity gives $Dv=Du$. Apply the local mean-zero estimate [[lem-mean-zero-poincare-estimate-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]] to get $\|v\|_p\le C_P\|Du\|_p$. Use the existing extension-domain embedding [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]] at $q=p^*$ to obtain $\|v\|_{p^*}\le C_E\|v\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_E(1+C_P)\|Du\|_p$ (with an equivalent norm constant if the selected Sobolev norm convention requires it). The proof retains exactly the source range $1<p<n$, and inherits choice only from its two suppliers. No later-page dependency occurs.

items.title: The critical Sobolev embedding into every finite $L^q$
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, open, bounded and a $W^{1,p}$-extension domain for every $p\in(n/2,n)$ (the extension operator may depend on $p$). For every $1\le q<\infty$ there is $C(n,q,\Omega)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,n}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,n}(\Omega;\mathbb K));$$
that is, $W^{1,n}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously for every finite $q$. The constant necessarily blows up as $q\to\infty$, so no $L^\infty$ bound is asserted.
items.strategy: For q≤n, Holder on the finite-measure domain gives the estimate from the L^n term. For q>n, set s=nq/(n+q)∈(n/2,n); the assumed W^{1,s}-extension property gives W^{1,s}→L^{s*}=L^q, while finite measure embeds W^{1,n} continuously into W^{1,s}. To show the constants diverge, localize the double-log W^{1,n} singularity in an interior ball; it is unbounded but lies in W^{1,n}, so its L^q norms tend to infinity on the finite-measure domain.

items.title: Ball-mean oscillation bound by the Riesz potential of the gradient
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $1\le p<\infty$, let $B(x,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a ball, and let $u\in W^{1,p}(B(x,r);\mathbb K)$ with ball average $u_{B(x,r)}$. Then
$$\bigl|u(z)-u_{B(x,r)}\bigr|\le C(n)\int_{B(x,r)}|Du(y)|\,|z-y|^{1-n}\,dy$$
for almost every $z\in B(x,r)$; here $|Du|$ is the Euclidean norm of the weak gradient and $C(n)$ depends only on $n$.
items.strategy: For $u\in C^1$ (Kinnunen's Lemma 5.22): $u(z)-u_B=\fint_B(u(z)-u(y))dy$; for $y\ne z$, write $u(y)-u(z)=\int_0^1Du(ty+(1-t)z)\cdot(y-z)dt$; integrate in polar coordinates centred at $z$ and change variables $w=ty+(1-t)z$ on the sphere $\partial B(z,\rho)$ with $dS(y)=t^{1-n}dS(w)$, $|w-z|=t|y-z|$; integrating the resulting expression in $\rho\in(0,2r)$ yields $|u(z)-u_B|\le c(n)\int_B|Du(y)||z-y|^{1-n}dy$. For $u\in W^{1,p}$, apply the $C^1$ bound to local smooth approximations $u_i\to u$ in $W^{1,p}(B)$; the truncated-kernel bound shows $I(|Du_i|\chi_B)\to I(|Du|\chi_B)$ in $L^p(B)$, and passing to an a.e.-convergent subsequence gives the bound a.e.

items.title: Morrey's inequality for $p>n$
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $n<p<\infty$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then $u$ has a continuous representative $u^{*}$, and for every ball $B(x,r)$ with $B(x,2r)\Subset\Omega$ one has
$$|u^{*}(z)-u^{*}(y)|\le C(n,p)\,|z-y|^{1-n/p}\,\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,2r))}\qquad(z,y\in B(x,r));$$
equivalently $[u^{*}]_{C^{0,1-n/p}(B(x,r))}\le C(n,p)\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,2r))}$.
items.strategy: For a.e. $z\in B(x,\rho)$ the previous lemma and Hölder (with $(n-1)p'<n$ because $p>n$) give $|u(z)-u_{B(x,\rho)}|\le C\rho^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,\rho))}$ for all $0<\rho\le r$. For $0<\rho,\sigma\le r$, comparing both balls through an intermediate ball contained in $B(x,r)$ gives $|u_{B(x,\rho)}-u_{B(x,\sigma)}|\le C\max(\rho,\sigma)^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,r))}$; hence the means are Cauchy as $\rho\downarrow0$ and $u^{*}(x)=\lim_{\rho\to0}u_{B(x,\rho)}$ exists with $|u^{*}(x)-u_{B(x,\rho)}|\le C\rho^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,r))}$. Lebesgue's differentiation theorem gives $u^{*}=u$ a.e., and the same comparison at scale $\rho=|z-y|$ inside $B(x,2r)$ gives the Hölder bound. Continuity on $\Omega$ follows by covering $\Omega$ with balls whose doubles lie in $\Omega$.

items.title: $W^{1,\infty}$ functions on convex domains have Lipschitz representatives
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded and convex. If $u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then $u$ has a representative $u^{*}$ with
$$|u^{*}(x)-u^{*}(y)|\le\|Du\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\,|x-y|\qquad(x,y\in\Omega),$$
and $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Conversely, every Lipschitz function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb K$ with constant $L$ lies in $W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le L$ for real scalars, while $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\sqrt2 L$ for complex scalars. In both cases the real-linear derivative has operator norm at most $L$ almost everywhere.

**Gradient convention.** For a weak gradient $Dv=(D_1v,\ldots,D_nv)$ we write $|Dv|=(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iv|^2)^{1/2}$ for its Euclidean norm and $\|Dv\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}:=\||Dv|\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for the essential supremum of that norm, as in [[lem-pointwise-potential-bound-for-compactly-supported-smooth-functions]]. For real scalars this norm equals the derivative operator norm. For complex scalars it is the Frobenius norm of the real-linear map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^2$ and can exceed its operator norm: $f(x)=x_1+ix_2$ is $1$-Lipschitz but $|Df|=\sqrt2$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ both assertions hold vacuously.
items.strategy: For the first direction, the ACL characterisation gives an absolutely continuous representative on a.e. line; for a.e. $x,y$ the segment $[x,y]$ lies in $\Omega$ and $|u(x)-u(y)|\le\int_0^1|Du(x+t(y-x))|dt\le\|Du\|_\infty|x-y|$. The ball means then satisfy $|\fint_{B(x,\rho)}u-\fint_{B(x,\sigma)}u|\le\|Du\|_\infty(\rho+\sigma)$ (compare through an intermediate ball), so $u^{*}(x)=\lim_{\rho\to0}\fint_{B(x,\rho)}u$ exists for every $x$, is $\|Du\|_\infty$-Lipschitz, and equals $u$ a.e. by Lebesgue's differentiation theorem. For the converse, a Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous on every line with $|f(x+te_j)-f(x+se_j)|\le L|t-s|$; its classical coordinate derivatives exist a.e. and are bounded by $L$, so applying the ACL characterisation with $p=1$ gives $f\in W^{1,1}(\Omega)$ with $D_jf$ the a.e. coordinate derivative; since that derivative lies in $L^\infty$ and $f$ is bounded on the bounded domain, $f\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ with $\|Df\|_\infty\le L$.

items.title: Weak partial derivatives lower the Sobolev order
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For every multi-index $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le k$ the weak derivative $D^{\beta}u$, viewed as an $L^p$ class, belongs to $W^{k-|\beta|,p}(\Omega)$, and $D^{\alpha}(D^{\beta}u)=D^{\alpha+\beta}u$ a.e. whenever $|\alpha|+|\beta|\le k$.
items.strategy: For $k=1$ and $|\beta|=1$, $D^{\beta}u\in L^p$ by definition and its weak derivative in a further coordinate direction $e_j$ is $D^{\beta+e_j}u$: the defining integration-by-parts identity for $D^{\beta+e_j}u$ is exactly the identity for the class $D^{\beta}u$ tested against $\partial_j\varphi$, by the commutation and locality properties of weak derivatives. Uniqueness of weak derivatives makes the construction representative-independent. The general case is induction on $k$ using this single step.

items.title: Higher-order Sobolev embedding
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
items.strategy: Iterate the first-order whole-space Sobolev inequality on a compactly supported W^{k,p} extension. In the supercritical case, descend derivative order while increasing the exponent until q>=n; if q>n, Morrey on a fixed ambient ball gives a closure-wide representative, with extra remaining derivatives allowing any larger finite q. If q=n, at least two derivatives remain and compact support plus Holder reduces w and Dw to W^{1,s} for s<n near n, after which Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev gives a supercritical exponent. Mollification proves consistency of the continuous derivative representatives.

items.title: Weak product rule for bounded Sobolev functions
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $u,v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$. Then $uv\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $D_j(uv)=(D_ju)v+u(D_jv)$ a.e. for every $j$.
items.strategy: Approximate: choose $u_k,v_k\in C^{\infty}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}$ with $u_k\to u$, $v_k\to v$ in $W^{1,p}$ and $\|u_k\|_\infty\le\|u\|_\infty$, $\|v_k\|_\infty\le\|v\|_\infty$ (local smooth approximation followed by truncation at $\pm\|u\|_\infty$, which preserves $W^{1,p}$ by the chain rule for globally Lipschitz maps). The classical Leibniz rule gives $D_j(u_kv_k)=(D_ju_k)v_k+u_k(D_jv_k)$. Hölder bounds $\|u_kv_k-uv\|_p\le\|u_k\|_\infty\|v_k-v\|_p+\|v\|_\infty\|u_k-u\|_p\to0$ and $\|D_j(u_kv_k)-[(D_ju)v+u(D_jv)]\|_p\to0$; closedness of the weak derivative operator transfers the identity to $uv$.

items.title: The Sobolev space $W^{k,p}$ is an algebra above the critical index
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.
items.strategy: Step 1.1 proves the multiplicative estimate for pairs of derivatives: for $w_1,w_2\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ and $|\gamma_1|+|\gamma_2|\le k$, the embedding places $D^{\gamma_i}w_i$ in $L^{q_i}$ with $\frac1{q_1}+\frac1{q_2}\le\frac1p$ (bounded factors when the remaining order exceeds $n/p$, every finite exponent at the critical order, and the Sobolev exponent below it), and Hölder bounds $\|D^{\gamma_1}w_1D^{\gamma_2}w_2\|_{L^p}\le C\|w_1\|_{W^{k,p}}\|w_2\|_{W^{k,p}}$. Step 2.1 chooses smooth $u_j,v_j$ converging to $u,v$ in $W^{k,p}$ by Meyers-Serrin, applies the classical Leibniz formula to the pairs $(u_j,v_j)$, passes each summand to the limit in $L^p$ by step 1.1, and identifies $\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}D^{\beta}u\,D^{\alpha-\beta}v$ as the weak $\alpha$-derivative of $uv$ through the test-function identity; summing over $|\alpha|\le k$ gives the asserted algebra inequality.

items.title: The $p=n$ endpoint: no $L^\infty$ or Holder embedding
items.statement:
Let $n\ge2$. On nonempty bounded $C^1$ domains in $\mathbb R^n$ (or domains satisfying the all-exponents extension hypothesis of the critical embedding theorem), $W^{1,n}$ embeds into $L^q$ for
every finite $q$ but not into $L^\infty$, and some $W^{1,n}$ classes have no representative in
$C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ for any $\alpha>0$. The exponential improvement
of Trudinger-Moser and the BMO/John-Nirenberg route to the same integrability
are outside this pair's scope and are recorded in the planning scope-denial
ledger; the companion page carries the witnesses.

The dimension restriction is essential: on a bounded interval $I$, every
$W^{1,1}(I)$ class has an absolutely continuous representative and satisfies
$\|u\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le |I|^{-1}\|u\|_{L^1(I)}+\|u'\|_{L^1(I)}$.
items.strategy: Statement-only remark. The witnesses and the failure of the uniform Holder bound are worked out on the B companion page; Trudinger-Moser and the BMO route are deliberately not built here.

items.title: Domain classes covered by the mean-zero Poincare inequality
items.statement: This page proves the mean-zero Poincare-Wirtinger inequality directly for bounded John domains [[thm-poincare-wirtinger-on-bounded-john-domains]] and for bounded convex domains [[cor-poincare-wirtinger-on-convex-domains]], both on the same page. Bounded $C^1$ and bounded Lipschitz domains satisfy the uniform interior cone condition, and every nonempty bounded connected open set satisfying that uniform condition is a John domain (Kinnunen, Remark 5.32(1)); hence the inequality applies to those classes as well. The John-class hypothesis $1\le p<\infty$ is the one used by the direct proof; no Sobolev exponent and no compactness input enter it. The bounded connected extension-domain Sobolev-Poincare form $1<p<n$ is a separate statement on this page, proved from the local mean-zero estimate and the extension-domain embedding, and it does not supersede the John-domain result.
items.strategy: Statement-only scope remark. PDE-14 proves the John and convex cases directly; PDE-15 proves the full bounded connected extension-domain claim without weakening its statement.

title: Sobolev Poincare and Morrey Inequalities — Examples

items.title: Dilations force the Sobolev conjugate
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$, and let $1\le q\le\infty$ and $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\setminus\{0\}$; for $\lambda>0$ put $u_\lambda(x):=u(\lambda x)$. Then
$$\|u_\lambda\|_{L^q}=\lambda^{-n/q}\|u\|_{L^q},\qquad\|Du_\lambda\|_{L^p}=\lambda^{\,1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p}.$$
If the inequality $\|u_\lambda\|_{L^q}\le C\|Du_\lambda\|_{L^p}$ is to hold for all $\lambda>0$ with a constant $C$ independent of $\lambda$, then the two powers of $\lambda$ must balance:
$$-\frac nq-\Bigl(1-\frac np\Bigr)=0,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad 1-\frac np+\frac nq=0,$$
which is equivalent to $q=\frac{np}{n-p}=p^{*}$. The exponent $p^{*}$ is therefore forced by scaling alone.
items.strategy: Change variables $y=\lambda x$ in both norms and compare the two powers of $\lambda$.

items.title: Poincare on an interval: the length dependence is linear
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $I=(0,L)$ with $L>0$ and let $1\le p<\infty$. For every $u\in W^{1,p}(I)$ with mean $u_I=|I|^{-1}\int_Iu$ one has
$$\|u-u_I\|_{L^p(I)}\le L\,\|u'\|_{L^p(I)} .$$
The dependence on $L$ cannot be improved below a positive multiple of $L$: for $u(x)=x-\frac{L}{2}$ the weak derivative is $u'\equiv1$, the mean vanishes, and
$$\|u-u_I\|_{L^p(I)}=L^{1+1/p}2^{-1}(p+1)^{-1/p},\qquad\|u'\|_{L^p(I)}=L^{1/p},$$
so the ratio $\|u-u_I\|_{L^p}/\|\text{u}'\|_{L^p}$ equals $c_pL$ with $c_p=\frac12(p+1)^{-1/p}>0$. Consequently every admissible constant for this family is at least $c_pL$, while the inequality above shows that $L$ itself is admissible: the optimal constant is of order $L$.
items.strategy: Upper bound: the absolutely continuous representative satisfies $|u(x)-u(y)|\le\int_I|u'|\le L^{1-1/p}\|u'\|_{L^p}$ for all $x,y$; Jensen gives $|u(x)-u_I|^p\le\fint_I|u(x)-u(y)|^pdy\le L^{p-1}\|u'\|_p^p$, and integrating over $x$ yields the bound. Lower bound: direct evaluation of the linear function's norms.

items.title: Poincare-Wirtinger fails on disconnected bounded domains
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega=B(0,1)\cup B(3e_1,1)\subset\mathbb R^2$ (two disjoint unit balls) and $u=\mathbf 1_{B(3e_1,1)}$. Then $Du=0$ almost everywhere and $u$ is not almost everywhere constant on $\Omega$, so $u-u_\Omega$ is nonzero on a set of positive measure and $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}>0$: the mean-zero Poincare-Wirtinger inequality is false on disconnected bounded open sets, and connectedness is essential for the single-global-mean normalisation.
items.strategy: Compute:$|\Omega|=2|B(0,1)|$, $u_\Omega=\frac12$, $\|u-u_\Omega\|=\frac12$ on each ball, so $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p}=2^{1/p}\cdot\frac12>0$, while $Du=0$.

items.title: A gradient-only Poincare estimate needs normalisation
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and $1<p<n$ with $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$, and let $\Omega$ be a nonempty bounded connected domain with smooth boundary. The following two assertions are false:

1. there is a finite constant $C$ with $\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. there is a finite constant $C$ with $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

A condition excluding nonzero constants is necessary; mean subtraction, zero trace, and vanishing on a set of positive measure are standard normalisations.
items.strategy: Take $\Omega=B(0,1)$ and $u\equiv1$. For each $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ extend the test by zero; Fubini and the one-dimensional FTC give $\int_\Omega\partial_i\varphi=0$, so every weak derivative of $u$ is zero. Both $u$ and its derivatives are in the required Lp spaces because the ball has finite positive measure. Its $L^{p^*}$ norm is $|\Omega|^{1/p^*}>0$, its $L^p$ norm is $|\Omega|^{1/p}>0$, and $\|Du\|_p=0$. Both proposed inequalities fail for every finite $C$. Subtracting the mean annihilates this witness.

references.title: Juha Kinnunen, Sobolev Spaces
references.locator: Theorem 3.47, printed pp. 90–91; explicit constant-function necessity witness.

items.title: The $W^{1,p}\to L^q$ bound fails for $q>p^{*}$ by dilation
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $q>p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. The assertion that there is a finite constant $C$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\qquad\text{for every }u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$$
is false. The stronger full-norm assertion $\|u\|_{L^q}\le C\|u\|_{W^{1,p}}$ also fails for this family, so the exponent $p^{*}$ is sharp for both estimates.
items.strategy: For finite q>p*, dilate a fixed nonzero smooth bump to small scales; the L^q-to-gradient ratio has exponent 1+n/q−n/p<0 and diverges. For q=∞, dilation preserves the essential supremum while the L^p gradient norm scales as lambda^(n/p−1), so the ratio diverges because p<n.

items.title: $W^{1,n}$ is not contained in $L^\infty$
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfy $0\le\varphi\le1$, $\varphi=1$ on $B(0,\frac12)$ and $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq B(0,2)$, and set $f(x)=\varphi(x)\log\log\bigl(1+\frac1{|x|}\bigr)$ for $x\ne0$, $f(0)=0$. Then $f\in W^{1,n}(\mathbb R^n)$ but $f$ is unbounded near the origin; therefore this $W^{1,n}$ class admits no bounded (and no continuous, let alone Holder) representative, and the endpoint $p=n$ has no $L^\infty$ embedding, while this compactly supported witness belongs to $L^q$ for every finite $q$ (the general bounded-domain finite-$q$ embedding is stated separately).
items.strategy: Let g be the double-log witness on B(0,1), and choose the stated cutoff φ. On B(0,1), φg is L^n; away from the origin it is smooth with compact support. Split φg as (χφ)g+(1−χ)φg for a smooth χ supported in B(0,1) and equal to one near 0. The first term has the weak product derivative on B(0,1) and extends by zero because χφ is compactly supported there; the second is smooth compactly supported away from 0. The resulting function is W^{1,n} and essentially unbounded, so no bounded representative exists; the finite-q contrast follows from the critical embedding.

items.title: Morrey's inequality has no $p=n$ endpoint
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$ and let $B=B(0,1)$. There are no constants $\alpha>0$ and $C$ with
$$[u]_{C^{0,\alpha}(B)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{1,n}(B)}\qquad\text{for every }u\in W^{1,n}(B);$$
that is, Morrey's inequality has no endpoint at $p=n$. The witness is
$$f(x)=\log\log\Bigl(1+\frac1{|x|}\Bigr)\quad(x\in B\setminus\{0\}),\qquad f(0)=0,$$
which lies in $W^{1,n}(B)$ but has no bounded representative. The hypothesis $p>n$ in Morrey's inequality is therefore essential.
items.strategy: Use the double logarithm on B(0,1). Near r=0, polar coordinates bound the L^n gradient integral by ∫_0^{1/2} dr/[r(log(1/r))^n], which converges for n≥2; on 1/2≤r<1 the exact radial derivative is bounded. The function is in L^n, and integration by parts on punctured balls identifies the weak gradient because the inner boundary term tends to zero. Its divergence near 0 excludes any bounded representative and hence any Holder representative on B.

items.title: Radial powers approach the Morrey borderline exponent
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $n<p<\infty$, $\alpha_0=1-\frac np\in(0,1)$, and for $0<\delta<\frac np$ define $u_\delta(x)=|x|^{\alpha_0+\delta}$ on $B=B(0,1)$, with $u_\delta(0)=0$. Then $u_\delta\in W^{1,p}(B)$ and
$$\|Du_\delta\|_{L^p(B)}=(\alpha_0+\delta)\Bigl(\frac{\sigma(S^{n-1})}{p\delta}\Bigr)^{1/p}.$$
The function $u_\delta$ is Holder of exponent $\alpha_0+\delta$ on $B$ with $[u_\delta]_{C^{0,\alpha_0+\delta}}=1$, and the local Morrey estimate holds on each $B(0,r)$ with $2r<1$; as $\delta\downarrow0$ the energy $\|Du_\delta\|_{L^p(B)}^p$ diverges like $\alpha_0^p\sigma(S^{n-1})/(p\delta)$, and the borderline function $|x|^{\alpha_0}$ is not in $W^{1,p}(B)$. The exponent $\alpha_0=1-\frac np$ is exactly the borderline produced by $p>n$.
items.strategy: For 0<δ<n/p, α=1−n/p+δ lies in (0,1). Compute the radial derivative and integrate |Du|^p in polar coordinates to obtain σ(S^{n−1})α^p/(pδ); the elementary Hölder inequality for r↦r^α gives seminorm 1. As δ↓0 the gradient energy has leading term α₀^pσ(S^{n−1})/(pδ), while the limiting borderline power has divergent derivative integral.

items.title: Outward dilation defeats subcritical inclusion and homogeneous Poincare on Euclidean space
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $0<q<p$. The assertions

1. $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)\hookrightarrow L^q(\mathbb R^n)$ continuously, and
2. the homogeneous Poincare inequality (even restricted to mean-zero functions) $\|u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$ for compactly supported smooth $u$,

are both false. In fact $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ is not even a subset of $L^q(\mathbb R^n)$. Although on bounded sets the inclusion $W^{1,p}\subseteq L^q$ for $q<p$ follows by applying Holder to $|u|^q$ and $1$ with exponents $p/q$ and $p/(p-q)$, on the whole of $\mathbb R^n$ even the full $W^{1,p}$ norm does not bound $L^q$ for $q<p$; additional quantitative decay or integrability assumptions would be needed. The whole-space inequality at $q=p^{*}$ is unaffected.
items.strategy: Change variables $y=x/k$ in both norms and let $k\to\infty$; the exponent $1+\frac nq-\frac np>0$ iff $q<p$.
